newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU harmonisation set to "reduce" Dutch inflation.
newsitem.headline: EU harmonisation set to "reduce" Dutch inflation.

text.p: An operation to harmonise EU consumer price statistics looks set to result in a much lower Dutch inflation rate than that calculated according to the current national definition.

Kees Buis of the consumer prices unit of the Dutch statistics office (CBS) said on Thursday the CBS and statistics offices in the other 14 EU states aim to start publishing harmonised consumer price indices from early March.
The harmonised EU inflation rates will be published alongside national figures rather than replace them, he added.
The move is needed to achieve a uniform measurement of EU states' performance on price stability, one of the so-called convergence criteria for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
The Maastricht treaty stipulates that to qualify for EMU, a country's inflation rate must be no more than 1.5 percentage points above that of the three countries with the lowest rates.
To approximate harmonised inflation rates, EU statistics offices have been calculating interim indices since January 1996 which strip out the national index components which differ most.

Figures published by the European Commission last November show that in September 1996 Dutch inflation was running at an annual rate of 2.0 percent according to the national definition but at only 1.4 percent according to the interim EU definition.
For March 1996 the Commission's report gave rates of 2.1 percent and 1.5 percent respectively according to the national and interim EU definitions.
Buis said that in the Netherlands' case the interim EU definition gave a fair indication of the official harmonised EU inflation figure which would eventually emerge.
"I think that it gives a reasonable indication...but there might be some further fine-tuning," he said.
Buis said the interim EU index covered about 75 percent of the goods and services included in the Dutch national index.
Local government taxes and charges, which have risen sharply in recent years, were excluded from the interim EU index and would probably remain outside the harmonised figures, he added.
The European Commission's figures showed a far smaller difference between neighbouring Germany's inflation figures according to the national and interim EU calculation methods.
For September 1996 they showed German inflation rates of 1.4 percent (national) and 1.3 percent (interim EU) and for March 1996 rates of 1.7 percent and 1.4 percent respectively.
